newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economic data paints mixed picture.
newsitem.headline: Japan economic data paints mixed picture.

text.p: Despite repeated official assurances that Japan's economy is on a "gradual recovery", the latest indicators paint a mixed picture as the negative effects of a tax rise begin to take a toll.

Industrial output figures for May, released on Friday, showed higher-than-expected growth, but retail sales figures released earlier this week show consumers have backed off since the consumption tax was raised to five percent from three on April 1.
And gloomy unemployment figures released on Friday followed a key central bank report on Wednesday which showed surprisingly high business confidence.
"As a trend, we believe that the economy is continuing its gradual recovery," Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita said in a speech on Friday.

Matsushita said the economy was highly likely to sustain its recovery trend, but added that the central bank needed to see actual movements in consumer spending and corporate activity to form a judgment.
But private consumption has been hit hard by the tax increase and businesses have also been affected.
Sales at department stores in Japan in May fell 5.1 percent from a year earlier and those at chain stores in May also dropped 4.6 percent from a year ago.

The Trade Ministry said on Friday that May industrial output rose a preliminary 3.8 percent from the previous month but forecast a 2.6 percent month-on-month fall in output for June and a mere 0.9 percent rise for July.

The May figure turned out to be above expectations, sparking an initial sell-off of Japanese government bonds (JGBs), but the market was quick to focus on the weak June and July numbers and bond prices skyrocketed by late trade.
The key September JGB futures finished Friday at 124.15, up 0.88 from Thursday after briefly rising as high as 124.27.
Similarly, other markets took more note of the weak outlooks, and the dollar rose over one full yen from its Thursday New York close while Tokyo shares ended down.

"May output data confirmed that the economic recovery was driven by the exporting sector. But the weak output forecast for June and July suggests that the Bank of Japan will remain quite wary of a credit tightening," said Yasunari Ueno, chief economist at Fuji Securities' research group.
The gloomy outlook of the economy was further fuelled by Friday's release of Japan's unemployment rate for May, which rose to 3.5 percent, matching the record high marked in May and June of 1996.

Gyrations in financial markets were made all the more wild as the weak indicators came right on the heels of a key corporate survey released on Wednesday which had showed a surprisingly upbeat Japanese business confidence.

The BOJ's quarterly "tankan" survey showed that confidence among the nation's major manufacturers was stronger than expected, fuelling speculation that the central bank may be closer than imagined to a credit tightening.
But on Friday, BOJ officials themselves tried to play down the brighter-than-expected results of the survey.
Eichiro Kinoshita, the BOJ's Osaka branch manager said there was no need for the central bank to alter its current assessment of the economy because of the tankan results.
"There are still many bearish factors," he said.
Kinoshita, also an executive director of the central bank, said the BOJ's current monetary policy of keeping interest rates low was still necessary.

"How low interest rates should be is a separate issue altogether, but at the moment, low interest rates are needed. As domestic demand is not strong enough, basically, there is a meaning for the low rate policy," he said.
